Artificial Intelligence Policy.
As of Fall 2025,
our course offers a new resource: the

CS 15 AI chatbot.

This is an LLM-backed
AI model that incorporates many of our course materials, and exists
to help you work through homeworks, projects, and studying for exams. It will
help guide you through problems, but
without
solving them for you,
thereby maximizing your learning and understanding in this course.
You can think of it as a teaching assistant that is available around-the-clock.

There are some important things to keep in mind when using the model:

Our chatbot, like any generative AI model,
can get things wrong!

It is ultimately your responsibility to verify the correctness of its
output. If you lose points on an assignment, you will not win them back
by blaming the chatbot. You are responsible for your own work.

On privacy: Please be aware that we will keep an
anonymous
log
of all interactions with the chatbot. This means that all conversations
will be saved, but instead of any identifying information (name, email, etc.),
we will save only a unique ID number for each chatbot user. Of course,
the contents of your interactions could reveal your identity, for example,
if you share a README file that includes your name; so please be mindful of
what you share.
We keep these logs so that we can review conversations in order to
inform future improvements to the chatbot.

The CS 15 chatbot is as new to us as it is to you. As we embark on this experiment,
we would love to hear any honest feedback you might have about it. Special thanks
to course assistants Muhammad Umair, Valentina Henao Giraldo, and Nahuel Gomez Ruiz
for spearheading this effort.

Finally, please note that
we disallow the use of all other generative AI models

including ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, Github Copilot, and similar models
when completing any assignment, lab, or exam.
This restriction applies to all work you produce
for this course: code, documentation, READMEs, etc. You are here
to learn as much as you can; you should not throw away this
opportunity by having AI models do your work for you. If we suspect that you have
submitted work that was generated by one of these models,
we may report you to Dean of Students office for an academic integrity investigation.

For Fall 2026, students will also need to purchase a Claude Pro subscription to use
Claude
Code
, an AI coding agent, for the
MP
.
You will work in the Claude desktop app’s Code tab, which requires a paid plan.

One month of Claude Pro

costs $20
.
The project runs from October 6 to December 10, a little over two months, so students should expect to purchase two to three months of access, for a total cost of $40–$60.

While there are cheaper and free options, we want CS 124 students to be exposed
to the best available AI technologies—so-called
frontier models
.
At present the best AI coding tools are both much, much better than inferior
approaches—like copying and pasting to ChatGPT—but also cost money.
Please see our
statement on AI
for more details.

All homework and quiz code you submit must be written by you.

Not by another student, not from the internet, and not by an AI assistant.
Hundreds of students work the same problems, so authorship is exactly the right standard here, and the quizzes are proctored precisely so that we can hold you to it.

To be clear about where the line falls: asking questions is fine, getting answers is not.
Use our
AI course assistant
to have a concept explained, ask a tutor to help you find your bug, talk a problem through with a classmate.
What you may not do is have any of them produce the code you turn in.
Every one of these problems is practice for a proctored quiz you will take without help, so a solution you did not write is practice you did not get.

Most courses define academic integrity by authorship: the work is yours if you wrote it.
The independent project does not work that way.
An AI agent will write most of your code, and that is the assignment, not a loophole.

What makes the project yours is everything the agent cannot do for you.
You decide what to build.
You direct the work and judge what comes back.
You put in the hours, and you come away understanding what you made.
Not every line of it—nobody expects you to recall a generated helper function months later—but what your app does, how it fits together, and why it is built the way it is.

So dishonesty here is not a question of who typed the code.
It is a question of whether you misrepresented your own engagement.
A good test:
if you can sit down with a tutor and walk them through your app—what it does, why it is built that way, what you tried that didn’t work—you are fine.

The standard
University of Illinois academic integrity policies
apply to the independent project, including your Claude Code session transcripts and the activity your Claude Code hooks report as you work.
Here is how each category of infraction applies:

Cheating:
Having someone else conduct Claude Code sessions on your behalf or otherwise complete your project work for you.

Plagiarism:
Directly copying another student’s code or Claude Code session logs and presenting them as your own.

Fabrication:
Editing, manufacturing, or otherwise tampering with Claude Code session logs, or with the activity your Claude Code hooks report, to misrepresent work you didn’t actually do. This includes using your project sessions for unrelated work, or any other attempt to inflate your measured hours.

Facilitation:
Sharing your Claude Code session transcripts, repository access, or verification codes with another student so they can submit your work as theirs.

Bribes, favors, and threats:
Attempting to influence project grading through inappropriate means.

Academic interference:
Tampering with another student’s repository, session transcripts, or project materials.

We will run automated checks on reported session activity, session transcripts, and code changes.
Evidence of any of the above will initiate academic integrity proceedings under the same policies described in our
general collaboration section
.

One thing that is
not
dishonest: setting your agent up on a long task and walking away.

Getting an agent to work productively without you hovering over it is a genuine skill, and we are not going to punish you for developing it.
But you also should not expect that time to count for much: each prompt earns at most ten minutes of the time Claude spends working on it.
Hours are measured by software, not judged by it.
Staff may review transcripts, and time spent on work that is not your project is removed.
The line is honesty about what happened: an agent working unattended on your project is a true transcript.
A transcript you edited, or project time spent on something that is not your project, is not, and may lead to a FAIR violation.

Responsible AI Usage
Responsible AI Usage

CS 124 teaches you to use AI coding agents to build software.
That pedagogical choice carries responsibilities.

AI is a powerful tool, and this course will give you real experience using it.
But the skills you develop here must be applied with judgment about context.
AI policies vary across courses, institutions, professions, and situations—and for good reasons.

AI Policies Vary Across Contexts
AI Policies Vary Across Contexts

In other courses
: Many instructors prohibit or restrict AI use, and these policies reflect legitimate pedagogical concerns.
When a professor asks you to write code or an essay without AI assistance, they are not being old-fashioned—they may be assessing your individual understanding, developing skills that require struggle, or maintaining equity among students with different levels of AI access.
The fact that you
can
use AI does not mean you
should
, and
violating another course’s AI policy is academic dishonesty regardless of what CS 124 permits
.

In professional contexts
: Some fields have strict requirements about AI use in documentation, research, or creative work.
Legal, medical, journalistic, and academic contexts may require disclosure of AI use, prohibit AI assistance entirely, or have evolving standards you will need to navigate.

In personal judgment
: Even where AI is permitted, you will need to decide when its use is appropriate.
Does using AI for this task serve your goals?
Does it align with your values?
Are you comfortable with the tradeoffs?

Your Responsibility
Your Responsibility

CS 124’s approach to AI is not a blanket endorsement of AI use everywhere.
We are teaching you
how
to use these tools effectively.
We are also teaching you to think critically about
whether
to use them.
Both skills matter.

You are always responsible for your own use of AI.

This means understanding and following the AI policies of every course you take, every organization you work for, and every context you operate in.
It means evaluating AI outputs critically rather than accepting them blindly.
And it means recognizing that AI systems create real costs—they consume enormous resources, they were trained on data collected without consent, and they can spread misinformation at scale.

AI is a powerful force.
Use it for good.

Throughout this policy, an
AI tool
is any generative system that produces code, text, or
explanations in response to a prompt, however you access it: through a chat interface, an editor extension, a
command-line tool, or an agent. Dictionaries, translation tools, spell checkers, and non-generative editor
completion are not AI tools under this policy and are always permitted. During a quiz, no tool beyond what the
testing environment provides falls within any permitted use. The governing prohibition appears under

Quiz Environment and Conduct
.

Using AI in this course is optional. You can complete every assignment and earn full marks without ever using an AI
tool. If you do use one, the rules in this policy apply.

The Standard

Our course standard is this: you must write your own code, and you must be able to explain every line of it. If a
course staff member asks why you wrote a particular line, what a specific variable represents, or how a section of
your code works, you should be able to answer immediately and confidently, without consulting any resource; if you
cannot, you have not yet learned what the assignment was designed to teach, regardless of whether your code
compiles and passes test cases. Stated as a rule of use, AI may support your process, e.g., understanding the
problem, learning relevant concepts, developing a strategy, debugging your attempts, and verifying correctness, but
it may not produce your product, i.e., the code you submit, which you must be able to reproduce independently.

Permitted Uses

You may use AI tools to assist your work on graded lessons, recitation activities, and machine problems in the
following ways:

Breaking down assignments:
Ask the AI to help you understand what an assignment is asking,
identify the component parts of the problem, and clarify requirements that seem ambiguous.

Developing a problem-solving plan:
Use the AI to help you formulate a high-level approach
before you begin writing code; that is, discuss algorithmic strategies, consider edge cases, and think through
the logical structure of your solution.

Explaining concepts or syntax:
When you encounter unfamiliar C++ constructs, language
features, or programming concepts, use the AI to help make sense of them.

Understanding error messages and debugging output:
Compiler errors and runtime failures can be
cryptic. The AI can help you interpret what went wrong and why.

Reviewing and explaining code:
After you have written code yourself, use the AI to help you
understand whether your implementation aligns with your intent and to identify potential issues.

Designing test cases:
Work with the AI to identify the scenarios, boundary conditions, and
expected behavior your tests should cover.

Test-case design carries a limit: because a test case in C++ is itself code, you may work from an AI tool's
suggestions, but you may not submit test code verbatim as an AI tool produced it.

Examples of Appropriate and Inappropriate Use

Appropriate and inappropriate AI prompts for CS 128 coursework, by situation.

When you are...

Appropriate

Inappropriate

Debugging a runtime error

"I'm getting a segmentation fault on line 23. Can you help me understand what might cause this?"

"My code has a segmentation fault. Fix it."

Learning a concept or language feature

"Can you explain how a destructor works in C++?"

"Write a destructor for my LinkedList class."

Tracing faulty logic in code you wrote

"I wrote this function but it's not returning the right value. Can you help me trace through the
logic?"

"This function doesn't work. Rewrite it so it works."

Designing test cases

"I want to test my reverse function but I'm not sure where to start. Can you help me understand the
process?"

"Generate all my test cases so I don't have to think about edge cases."

Beginning an assignment

"I'm not sure how to approach this problem. Can you help me break it down into smaller steps?"

"Here's the assignment prompt. Write the solution."

Vibe Coding and Other Prohibited Use

Vibe coding
is the practice of prompting an AI until something works, without ever solving the
problem yourself. It is an academic integrity violation in this course, as is any other arrangement in which the AI
does your work for you. Two conditions govern every use of AI on CS 128 coursework, and both must hold: you must solve the problem, and you must understand every line you submit.

The first condition concerns who does the work. A request that hands the problem to the AI fails this condition at
the moment you make it, and understanding the result afterward does not repair the failure, since arriving at the
solution is the work the assignment existed to develop. Test code is the exception, and Permitted Uses above states
its limit. The following requests are violations:

Asking the AI to complete an assignment or produce a solution for you.

Asking the AI to "write a function that does X," or making any comparable request for solution code you should
be writing yourself.

Asking the AI to "make this work" or "fix this" in place of diagnosing the problem yourself.

The second condition concerns what you submit. Everything you turn in must be yours to explain, line by line,
without consulting your notes or the AI. This condition applies equally to code you wrote entirely on your own. The following are violations:

Submitting code you cannot fully explain.

Iteratively prompting the AI until the tests pass, without comprehending what changed or why.

In a previous semester, we flagged approximately 150
students whose submissions exhibited patterns consistent with AI-generated code produced with minimal
understanding. Their median quiz score was 30 percentage points lower than that of students who were not flagged,
and the median score of those who relied most heavily on AI-generated submissions fell below passing.

Submitting the required reflection form and transcript does not excuse a violation of these conditions; we refer
such violations to FAIR regardless.

Required Documentation

For every graded lesson, recitation activity, and machine problem on which you use AI assistance, however minimal
or extensive, you must submit the
AI Usage Reflection Form
together with the complete transcript
of your AI interactions. The form is at

cs128.org/go/ai-reflection
,
and it requires you to log in with your UIUC account.

To access this form, you will need to use your Illinois G Suite account.

If you haven't activated it (most of you probably did in CS 124), kindly review
these instructions
.

The major step is activating the account in the
Cloud Dashboard
.

If you did not use AI on a particular assignment, you do not
need to submit the form. The form asks
you to document which tools you used and for what purposes, what you learned from the interaction, how you verified
that you understood the AI's suggestions, and what you would do differently next time, and to upload your
transcripts.

Save your transcripts as follows.

Command-line tools
, e.g., Claude Code: we encourage you to use

specstory-cli

(specstory.com/specstory-cli), which automatically logs your conversations so that they can be exported for
submission. If you choose not to use it, save the session output yourself, either by capturing the terminal
session to a file or by copying the conversation into a text file as you work.

Browser-based tools:
download the entire conversation using the platform's export or download
feature, or copy the full conversation into a text or PDF file where no export exists.

Multiple sessions or tools on one assignment:
submit transcripts from all sessions, labeling
each with the tool used and the date and time of the session.

Inline code-completion tools
that cannot produce a transcript, e.g., GitHub Copilot, may not be
relied on for coursework in this course.

Never ask the AI to reproduce the conversation for you: an AI asked to output a transcript produces a summary or a
paraphrase, and the attestation you sign requires a complete and unaltered record.

Some assignments specify a required prompt header or interaction protocol, e.g., an opening prompt that establishes
context or constraints for the AI conversation. Where an assignment specifies such a requirement, you must follow
it; failing to do so is a violation of this policy.

Submit the AI Usage Reflection Form by 23:59 Champaign local time the day after you submit the work, or on the
last day of instruction, whichever is earlier. For work you submit late, the clock runs from your actual
submission.

Attestation

By submitting the AI Usage Reflection Form, you affirm that:

The information provided on the form is accurate and complete.

The submitted transcript(s) represent the complete and unaltered record of your AI interactions for this
assignment.

You understand that AI tools are permitted to support your learning, but that you are responsible for ensuring
that you understand all work you submit.

You acknowledge that quizzes must be completed without AI assistance and that your performance on quizzes
reflects your genuine understanding of the course material.

Tools and Cost

We want you exposed to the most capable AI technologies, i.e., the frontier models, and we want you to develop the
habit of using them effectively and responsibly while you are still in an environment where we can guide that
development. We recommend Claude. Other tools such as ChatGPT or Gemini may also be used in accordance with this
policy. No purchase is required: the free tiers of these tools are sufficient for every use this policy
permits.

Generative AI tools can provide plausible text or code, but they do not replace your learning. This course seeks to impart and measure a solid understanding of course material rather than your knack in prompting a model.

Improper use of AI tools can:

Mask gaps in your understanding

Lead to incorrect or unverified solutions

Cause poor performance in unplugged exams and interviews

Warning
WARNING

AI usage is not allowed in individual assessments (i.e., quizzes and exams). Any use of AI tools in these assements is a breach of class policy.

That said, we recognize that generative AI tools can be useful for brainstorming, ideation and additional learning. You may sparingly use generative AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, GitHub Copilot, Bard) to assist your learning and problem solving.

We strongly recommend a maximal attempt to solving problems yourself before resorting to LLM use.

Your AI usage in this class is subject to the following guidelines:

You must re-write:
all solutions, code, explanations based solely on
your understanding
without help after AI usage.

Simply copying text or code from an AI tool into your submission (even with attribution) is
NOT
acceptable.

Simply reading the AI generated solution is
NOT
learning.

Simply paraphrasing the AI solution while having it open is
NOT
based on
your understanding.
Go for a run, have a meal – come back and then redo the problem
by yourself
.

While we won’t enforce this guideline any deviation from it will naturally become obvious (see point 3 above).

Like Prof. Erickson
writes
,
“…
Understanding
is a seductive lie, a warm feeling of satisfaction that your brain uses as a defense mechanism against doing real work. The only way to know when
when
you truly understand the concepts (is) when you can do the work.”

So, if after using AI, you cannot solve a problem of the same pattern on your own, you have
not
learned the material.

You must clearly document usage of the tool
: On any submitted work where AI usage is allowed, include a short statement at the top or bottom of your submission. For example:

Used ChatGPT (GPT-4) to help interpret problem prompt and brainstorm
approaches; final solution written entirely in my own words."

Treat AI assistance like any other external source
: Use it to inform your work instead of generating it.
Always validate it independently.
Then, cite any usage, and describe/reflect on how you used it to inform your work or better your understanding.

The days of being able to pass AI work off as your own could soon be over. See
Anthropic’s announcement
about watermarking AI generated
text
.

As engineers and computer scientists, you are expected to be responsible for all documentation and code you submit, and to ensure that it is correct & complete – you will hardly be able to blame AI for a failure at your future workplace.

GenAI policy: Generative AI tools may be used in this course as a learning aid, such
as for explaining concepts, debugging, identifying errors, or providing suggestions.
However, students may not use AI to generate an entire solution or submit AI-
generated code as their own work. Students are responsible for understanding,
verifying, and being able to explain all code they submit, and should disclose AI use
when it materially contributes to their work.

Recent advances in generative AI require us to adapt the way in which we teach and assess students
in all disciplines of computer science. Current coding agents such as Codex or Claude can produce
fully working artifacts for structured course projects with little or no human intervention, solely on
the basis of detailed specifications like the ones we typically prepare for such projects. As a result,
we must minimize longer use code artifacts created in unproctored environments to assess the skills
or level of mastery of students.
That said, we continue to believe that projects that require you to apply the systems-level concepts
you’re exposed to in the context of specific requirements, environments, and system designs, and
that result in deliverables are very likely to be beneficial, if not necessary, to achieve the level of
skills and understanding of systems we (and future employers) expect CS graduates to possess.
For this reason, our approach is fourfold:
1. We continue to include projects that are designed to be implemented by humans with minimal
or no AI support.
2. We will allow the use of AI assistants for these projects, but (not yet) require their use.

3. We will grade these projects based on functionality and correctness.
4. We will increase the number of unassisted, proctored assessments (exams and quizzes). Part
of these assessments will assume, and be specifically designed to test understanding that we
believe can only be gained by having worked on the projects in the manner we recommend:
namely, by using AI as an assistant, not by becoming an assistant to AI.
